examples: Thanks to my teacher, I was able to pass the exam for my first-choice school.
Thanks to my friend helping me, I finished early.
Thanks to the good weather, we were able to fully enjoy the picnic.
Thanks to the new tool, work efficiency went up.
Thanks to the traffic jam, I was late for an important meeting.
Thanks to all of you, we were able to complete the project successfully.
fields.explain:
Formal/polite when expressing gratitude: used together with ～おかげです／本当にありがとうございますと併用.
Avoid using it with bad results in formal written language; for negative cases, use ～せいで.
With positive objective events (天気、制度、技術), it is used naturally.
About yourself, avoid self-praise: ×自分のおかげで成功した → 〇皆さんのおかげで成功した。

• States a positive cause: “thanks to … (good result)”.
• Can also be used ironically/negatively in spoken language: “…のおかげで (against one's wishes)”, but be careful with the nuance.
• Implies gratitude toward the person/cause that helped achieve the result.
• Can be used with people, things, conditions, or circumstances as long as they bring a benefit.
fields.notes:
• おかげさまで is a set phrase used when someone asks after you: “Thanks to heaven/Thanks to everyone, I'm doing well”.
• In formal speeches, end with ～おかげです to express gratitude.
• In spoken language, ironic use needs to be weighed against the context to avoid being impolite.
meaning_vi: Thanks to… / Because of… (usually a good result)
explain: States the cause leading to a result (usually good) to express appreciation or gratitude; sometimes used ironically.
examples: 1. 仕事が早く済んだのは、友だちが手伝ってくれたおかげだ。
The work got done early thanks to my friends helping me.
2. 白髪が少ないおかげで若く見られることが多い。
Thanks to having few gray hairs, I am often seen as younger.
3. 医療技術の進歩のおかげで平均寿命が伸びた。
Thanks to advances in medical technology, average life expectancy has increased.
4. 彼の言うことを信じたおかげでひどい日にあった。
Because I believed what he said, I had a terrible day.
5. 「お母様の具合はいかがですか」「おかげさまで、すっかり良くなりました」
How is your mother doing? — Thanks to heaven, she has fully recovered.
explain: Used to mention a good result brought about by some event or person. (reason)
Implies gratitude
examples: 1. 先生のおかげで合格できました。
Thanks to my teacher, I passed
2. 日本へ来たおかげで、日本語が上手になった。
Thanks to coming to Japan, my Japanese got better
「～の影響で…といういい結果になる（おかげだ）/よくない結果になる（せいだ）。」 …には希望・意向・相手への働きかけなどの文は来ない。
Due to the influence of ~, it leads to a good result (thanks to) / leads to a bad result (because of)
… does not take sentences expressing a desire, intention, or a request for the other person to do something.
1. いい会社に就職が決まったのは先生のおかげです。ありがとうございました。
I got a job at a good company thanks to you, sensei. Thank you very much.
2. 天気のいい日が続いたおかげで、工事が早く終わった。
Thanks to a stretch of days with good weather, the construction finished early.
3. 最近忙しかったせいで、かなり疲れている。
Because I've been busy lately, I'm quite tired.
mistakes: Using おかげで for a bad result in formal writing → switch to せいで.
Wrong combination: ×親切のおかげで → 〇親切なおかげで.
Confusing the nuance with ために: exams often ask you to choose between おかげで (positive) and せいで (negative).
Self-praise: ×自分のおかげで成功した (unnatural, lacking modesty).

fields.meaning: Half-done…, in the middle of doing | Unfinished, incomplete
examples: There is a half-read book on the desk.
I tore the half-written letter to shreds.
That fish was dying, but somehow it survived.
Just when I had almost forgotten, I heard from him.
It was starting to rain, so I hurried home.
Just as I was about to go out, the home phone rang.
fields.explain:
The form “Vます + かけのN” is very common when describing unfinished things (食べかけのパン).
When it means “almost”, it often goes with verbs on the border of life/death or losing/gaining (死にかける、忘れかける).
The nuance can be negative (left unfinished) or neutral/urgent (almost, about to).
Not used for situations that are already completed; for completion, switch to Vてしまう/V終える.
In descriptive writing, 〜かけだ expresses a state:夕立が始まり かけだ （an evening shower is about to start）.

• Meaning 1: “Half-done, only partly done” → emphasizes that it is not completed.
• Meaning 2: “About to/almost …” → a state at the threshold of strongly happening (approaching).
• Different from an ordinary action in progress: 〜ている expresses doing; 〜かける emphasizes being unfinished/incomplete or almost.
• Usually attaches to verbs with a process (読む、書く、食べる、忘れる、壊れる...).
• Unnatural with purely punctual verbs when meaning “half-done” (×決めかける in the sense of “half-decided” is usually avoided; use 決めかけたところで if you want to emphasize the threshold).
fields.notes:
• In many cases 〜かける is fixed: 焼けかける、壊れかける、忘れかける.
• In conversation, 〜かけて（いた/いる） is used flexibly to emphasize a process that is not finished.
• “Vます + かけ” itself is also used as a noun in spoken language: やりかけ（a task left half-done）.
• Avoid redundancy: ×読みかけている本（wordy）; natural: 読みかけの本.
meaning_vi: Unfinished state, not yet done
explain: Expresses a state of being half-done, not completed.
examples: 1. 書きかけの手紙
A half-written letter
2. 読みかけの本
A half-read book
3. 食べかけのりんご
A half-eaten apple
4. 忘れかけていた記憶
A fading memory (almost forgotten)
5. 「やりかけたことは最後までちゃんとやりなさい」
Finish properly, all the way to the end, what you have left half-done.
6. 彼女は何か言いかけたが、すぐに口を閉じてしまった。
She started to say something but immediately closed her mouth.
meaning_vi: 全部～し終わっていない
Have not finished ~ entirely
examples: 1. 彼女は何か言いかけて、黙ってしまった。
She started to say something, then fell silent.
2. 母は読みかけの本をおいて、買い物に出かけた
My mother put down the book she was in the middle of reading and went out shopping.
meaning_vi: Not finished, incomplete
explain: Used when an action is still being carried out (even if not continuously) and has not completely ended
examples: 1. この本はまだ読みかけだ。
I am still in the middle of reading this book.
2. おふろに入りかけたときに電話が鳴った。
The phone rang just as I was getting into the bath
meaning_vi: Not finished, still incomplete
examples: 1. 読みかけの本が何冊もある。
I have several books I'm in the middle of reading.
2. 彼女は何か言いかけてやめた。
She started to say something and then stopped.
3. 私は、子どものとき、病気で死にかけたことがある。
When I was a child, I nearly died from an illness.
mistakes: Using it with punctual actions: ×着きかけだ → 〇着いたところだ／着きそうだ (depending on the intended meaning).
Confusing it with ～ている: “食べている” means eating now; “食べかけだ” means half-eaten (stopped before finishing).
Confusing “almost” with そうだ: 壊れかけ (has already deteriorated and is close to breaking) ≠ 壊れそう (looks like it is about to break).
JLPT: often tests the noun phrase “V-かけのN” and the negative nuance of “死にかける”.

fields.connection: V plain form + かな / N / Na / Aい
examples: I wonder if it's okay to leave this luggage here?
At first, I thought it might be impossible for me.
fields.explain: ◎ A sentence pattern used when talking to yourself, expressing a slight feeling of doubt. Because it sounds like a monologue, it gives a lively feeling.
fields.notes: Formed by adding 「な」 to 「か」, which expresses a question; used at the end of a sentence, it expresses the feeling of asking oneself. When talking to oneself it expresses wonder or doubt, but when directed at a listener it is a statement of doubt, and from that it can also express an indirect request for permission or a request. It is not attached to the polite style. Casual speech. It is sometimes pronounced with a lengthened ending as 「…かなあ」.（８１）

examples: From October to November, you can see beautiful autumn leaves.
Snow will probably fall from the Tohoku region through Hokkaido.
Around here, various flowers bloom from April to May.
Due to the typhoon, heavy rain continued to fall from last night through this morning.
This plant can be seen from northern to central Kyushu.
In the gas explosion, he suffered severe burns from his shoulder to his hip.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes “an approximate range” or “stretching across”; avoid using it with overly precise points in time (3時から4時にかけて can still be used but implies “approximately/not exactly on the hour”).
Often appears with phrases such as:広い範囲で／見込みだ／続く／観測した／かけて.
Neutral style, suitable for news and explanatory writing.

• Expresses a period of time/area of space that “stretches out” and is “not entirely precise”.
• Often used with phenomena that last or spread: rain, wind, traffic jams, fever, flower seasons, events.
• Not suitable when a precise point is needed; in that case use から～まで.
• The nuance of reporting, forecasting, and announcing (news, weather) is very common.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～から～まで.
→ ～から～にかけて indicates a “rough” scope and does not state the boundary as clearly as ～まで.
2) Often used for times/places that have some width.
→ It means “from around A to around B”.
3) Not used when you want to emphasize the exact end point.
→ If you need to emphasize “exactly up to B”, prefer ～まで.
meaning_vi: Indicates a general scope of place or time.
examples: 1. ①　８月から９月にかけて
From August to September
2. ②　このブドウは、８月から９月にかけて収穫されます。
These grapes are harvested from August to September.
3. ③　あすは、北海道から東北地方にかけて、強い風が吹くでしょう。
Tomorrow, strong winds will probably blow from Hokkaido to the Tohoku region.
meaning_vi: From…(stretching) to…
explain: Used when describing a period of time/area of space whose start and end points are not precisely defined
examples: 1. 明日は昼から夕方にかけて雨でしょう。
Tomorrow it will probably rain from noon through the evening.
2. 九州から本州にかけて梅雨入りました。
The rainy season has begun from Kyushu to Honshu.
meaning_vi: From around ～ to around ～
explain: Used for both scope and time.
examples: 1. 私は、２００７年から２００９年にかけて、ロンドンに住んでいました。
I lived in London from 2007 to 2009.
2. この駅から、あそこの通りにかけて、再開発されるそうです。
I hear the area from this station to that street over there will be redeveloped.
mistakes: Confusing it with まで: if the exam asks for “approximate” → choose にかけて; “precise” → choose まで.
Using it for a one-off action (一回だけ) → Unnatural. It should be a phenomenon that lasts or spreads.
Using it with nouns that are not time/space → Wrong scope of usage.

examples: Today I'll drink tea instead of coffee.
Instead of eating out, I save money by cooking at home.
I will attend the meeting in place of my father.
This apartment is far from the station, but in exchange the rent is cheap.
I'll help you, but in return, treat me to a meal next time, okay?
I have more free time now, but in exchange my income has unfortunately gone down.
fields.explain:
N の かわりに : used when replacing a specific thing/person/task, or acting on someone's behalf.
Vる/Vない + かわりに : emphasizes choosing an alternative course of action.
Aい/Aな + かわりに : states a contrasting feature to balance advantages/disadvantages, with a nuance of “compensation”.
When it means “in exchange”, the first clause and the second clause usually stand in a contrast of equal degree.
Do not use かわりに when simply listing two features that have no compensating relationship.

• Replacement/instead of: A かわりに B = instead of A, B; or using B in place of A.
• In exchange/to compensate: A かわりに B = A has an advantage/disadvantage, and to compensate there is B (corresponding nature).
• On behalf of/representing: N のかわりに V = do something in place of N (because N is busy/absent).
• Nuance: emphasizes a relationship of exchange/correspondence (trade-off); can be used in both spoken and formal written language.
• Spelling: かわりに is often written 代わりに; both are acceptable.
fields.notes:
• “AかわりにB” is sometimes understood as “in exchange for B” (a transactional meaning), especially with てあげる/てもらう.
• Written language tends to prefer 代わりに; conversation uses both, and かわりに is softer.
• Do not use かわりに in place of 「～の代理で」 when extreme formality is needed (legal documents use 代理/代行).
• Merged from 3 entries: (Shinkanzen), 1103 (Marugoto grammar_n3, the original grammar point has the typo ～わかりに), 1161 (Somatome — split into a separate entry ～そのかわり(に)).
Shinkanzen 18 divides it into 4 usages: ①②③ there is ~, but on the other hand there is also … to an equal degree; ④ instead of doing ~ as usual, do … as a substitute.
Mimikara 86 — tip for distinguishing the 3 meanings: an exchange of benefits → "in exchange"; A does something in someone's place → "in place of/on behalf of"; two contrasting sides → "although… on the other hand". Easily confused with ～に代わって (separate grammar point, currently no. 1036).
explain: ◎ Doing the task of another person or thing.
examples: 1. 友だちの かわりに、わたしがアルバイトをしました。
I worked the part-time job in place of my friend.
mistakes: Mistaking “contrast” for “compensation”: not every pair of opposites can take かわりに unless there is an equivalent exchange relationship.
Dropping 「の」 before かわりに with a noun: it must be N のかわりに, not N かわりに.
Confusing it with ために: かわりに does not state a purpose. A sentence like ×健康のかわりに運動する is incorrect.
JLPT: often tests distinguishing “AかわりにB” (in exchange) from “A一方B” (on the other hand).

examples: People tend to think that Japanese people are serious and quiet.
On days with bad weather, trains tend to be late.
Maybe because of her age, my mother has been getting sick a lot lately.
Trains in the 7 a.m. and 8 a.m. hours tend to be late.
The weather has been mostly cloudy for days, so the laundry won't dry.
When you live alone, your nutrition tends to become unbalanced.
fields.explain:
Has a slightly negative/undesirable nuance; avoid using it directly about the listener if it might cause offense.
Can be used for people, things, weather, and health.
Not used for a process in progress at the moment of speaking (that is ～ている); ～がち talks about a general tendency.
Often accompanied by frequency adverbs for reinforcement: どうしても、つい、最近は….

• Expresses a tendency “often …, tend to …”, mostly with a negative/undesirable nuance.
• Applies to habits, repeated situations, and temporary tendencies within a certain period.
• Not used for a single specific event; there needs to be repetition or a tendency.
• Compared with ～やすい: ～がち emphasizes “a result that often happens” rather than “something that easily happens due to its nature”.
fields.notes:
• Grammatically, ～がち is originally a suffix attached after a noun/ren’youkei (Vます), forming an adjective meaning “having a tendency”.
• In describing weather/the economy, ～がち is used to state a short-term tendency: 雨がち、値下がりがち.
• It is more polite when talking about others: ～がちですね instead of a harsh judgment. meaning_vi: Have a tendency to~, usually~ ⏐ explain: Used to express the meaning of having a tendency, often happening…and the matter described tends to be undesirable.Similar to the sentence pattern ～嫌いがある。 ⏐ examples: 1. 私は子どもの頃、病気がちだった。
As a child, I was often sick.
2. 最近、彼は仕事を休みがちだ。
Lately, he tends to take days off work.
mistakes: Using it for a single event: Incorrect. ～がち requires repetition/a tendency.
Confusing it with ～やすい: ～がち means “often happens”, not “easy to do”.
Forgetting to change the verb to Vます before ～がち (×忘れるがち → ○忘れがち).
Using it with a praising nuance: usually inappropriate because ～がち is mostly negative.

I was so busy today that I didn't even have time to eat lunch. All I had was some milk in the morning.

～だけ（limitation）
fields.explain:
Vた + きり : the second clause is usually negative or a continuing state (～ない/～ていない/～まま).
“Only/sole”: can be combined with しか～ない for more emphasis (一度きりしか～ない).
っきり: used with family/friends; avoid in formal documents.
Different from “だけ”: きり emphasizes a stricter limitation, with the feeling “just that, nothing more”.

• Only/sole: Limits the amount/target to exactly what is stated (a narrowing nuance, sometimes with regret).
• Since V, (still) not…: Describes a situation after a past event that continues to the present, usually with a negative in the second clause.
• Colloquial っきり: natural in conversation, casual; きり is more formal/neutral.
• Often attached in pairs such as 夫婦きり, 二人きり, 子どもきり, etc. to emphasize that it is only that exact group.
fields.notes:
• Vたきり can go with “そのまま”, implying it naturally continues: 出たきり（そのまま）帰らない.
• “N + きりで” sometimes drops “で”: 夫婦きり暮らしている（＝夫婦きりで暮らしている） in spoken language.
• In headlines/advertising, 一度きり emphasizes a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity”.
mistakes: Using きり with the present tense for the meaning “since”: it must be Vたきり, not Vるきり.
Confusing きり with だけ: in JLPT questions, きり usually carries a stronger sense of narrowness/uniqueness.
Forgetting the negative in the second clause with Vたきり when you want to say “since then, not …”: ～ない/～ていない is needed.
Confusing きり with っぱなし: っぱなし means “leave as is” and does not mean “since”.
